mangroves: Why the roots change the shore
Start with the stilt-like root network and follow what happens to tidal water and sediment.

Many mangrove forests have prop roots. The roots slow tidal waters, allowing sediment to settle and build up the muddy bottom. They also offer shelter to organisms. Most mangroves flood at least twice per day.
Keep ‘many’ and ‘most’ distinct. Reduced erosion is not complete protection.
ripcurrent: Two currents with easily confused names
Use the two names to clarify where each type of flow occurs and what distinguishes them.

NOAA describes rip currents as powerful narrow channels of fast-moving water, present along U.S. ocean coasts and Great Lakes shores, moving at up to eight feet per second. A rip tide describes swift tidal water through inlets and certain mouths.
Treat the speed as an upper bound, not a usual speed. Center the distinction in names and locations.
stormsurge-stormtide: What the storm adds to the water level
Start with the observed water level, then unpack the predicted tide and storm-driven increase.

Storm surge is measured above the normal predicted astronomical tide and is caused primarily by storm winds pushing water onshore. Storm tide is their combination. Track relative to coast, storm characteristics and bathymetry affect surge amplitude.
Coincidence with new or full moon can raise storm tide. Do not make lunar phase a cause of the storm-driven surge.
upwelling: Why surface water can be replaced from below
Follow the displaced surface water, then trace the biological significance of what replaces it.

Wind pushes surface waters away. Deeper, typically colder and nutrient-rich water rises to replace them. Nutrients often support high biological productivity. The reverse process may sink water that builds up along a coast.
Keep biological productivity and fishing grounds as typical or common associations, not promises.
sound: A whale call through changing water
Use the article’s hypothetical call to follow bending sound paths through layers of different temperature and pressure.

In the example sound slows and refracts downward as temperature drops. Near the bottom of the thermocline sound speed reaches a minimum; deeper, temperature remains stable and increasing pressure raises speed, bending the sound upward. Hydrophones at a suitable depth can detect distant signals.
Keep the whale example illustrative and avoid making a universal distance claim.
conveyor: A current with a return route
Follow the cold sinking water through the deep return route, ending with how the cycle continues.

NOAA’s illustration traces water losing heat in the Norwegian Sea, becoming denser and sinking. Cold bottom water moves south across the equator toward Antarctica and eventually returns to the surface through mixing and wind-driven upwelling. Deep thermohaline and wind-driven surface currents contribute to circulation.
A depicted ‘start’ is an editorial entry into a continuing system, not its historical beginning.
geodesy: Why port measurements share a reference
Use the clearance under a bridge to make an abstract measurement discipline concrete.

Geodesy measures Earth’s geometric shape, orientation and gravity field. NOAA describes tides and bridge clearance measurements tied to a common reference as one example of systems supporting port travel.
Do not attach measurements to a specific named port or quantify benefits without evidence.
bluecarbon: Start with unseen carbon in coastal soils, then connect storage to the consequences of habitat damage.

NOAA identifies sea grasses, mangroves and salt marshes as coastal sinks. Most of the carbon taken up by those ecosystems is stored below ground. Damage can release stored carbon back into the atmosphere.
Do not convert an account of storage into a quantified mitigation guarantee or claim all blue carbon is soil carbon.
